hook_text: Cape Town gets its rain in winter, like Rome. Antarctica is a desert. Here is why.
clip_script: Some climates are extreme. Deserts get less than two hundred and fifty millimetres of rain a year: the Sahara, the Namib, and in the Northern Cape, Upington with about one hundred and ninety. Cape Town breaks South Africa's pattern: rain in winter from cold fronts, dry summers under high pressure. That is a Mediterranean climate, shared with Italy, California and Perth, and it grows fynbos. Deep inside Russia, Moscow swings from about nineteen degrees in summer to about minus six in winter: continental. Near the Arctic, the tundra has frozen ground and no trees. And Antarctica, coldest place on earth at about minus eighty-nine, gets so little snow that it counts as a desert.
visual_style: A whiteboard world map with quick sketches popping up: a cactus, a Cape protea in rain, a snowy onion-domed city, moss on frozen ground, and an ice sheet with a thermometer at minus eighty-nine.
pacing: Rapid-fire, one image per climate, with a surprise at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and match each climate to its place.
